explainBack.question: Why does the House's 417–3 passage of H.R. 9340 not change anyone's electricity bill yet?
explainBack.answer: Because a one-chamber vote sits early on the decision chain: the Senate has not passed it (a September 17 unanimous-consent attempt drew an objection), and even after enactment the bill would only require state regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider and determine a standard for sites with at least 100 megawatts of peak demand. A household bill changes only when a specific utility's rate design is later approved under that consideration.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The Washington section: 'The bill would require consideration and a determination; it would not itself set one nationwide retail rate' plus the Senate objection and the 100 MW threshold in P002, and the decision-chain framing in P003.
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this causal explanation in ordinary language; every link (chamber vote, objection, consideration duty, threshold, later rate design) is explicit in P002 and P003.

The manager should check who is covered (the spending threshold), the stated effective date in the final adopted text, and any national implementing rules — the same way the article told readers a House vote still needs enactment and a local rate decision.
